stem:
A 47-year-old woman tells her GP that for several months she has felt tired all the time, her face looks puffy, her periods have become heavier and she feels the cold more than her colleagues. She has no previous thyroid disease and takes no medicines. The GP wants to check whether her thyroid is underactive.

Which single blood test is usually requested first?
why_correct: TSH is the most sensitive first-line test for primary thyroid dysfunction because the pituitary amplifies small changes in thyroid hormone levels. If the TSH is abnormal, free T4 is measured, often automatically by the laboratory, to confirm and grade the problem. This approach is recommended for suspected hypothyroidism in someone without pituitary disease.
why_wrong: A. Free T3 adds little in suspected hypothyroidism and is more useful in hyperthyroidism. C. Antibodies help identify an autoimmune cause once dysfunction is confirmed but are not the screening test. D. Thyroglobulin is used to monitor thyroid cancer after treatment. E. Free T4 alone is less sensitive and misses subclinical disease.
pearl: If pituitary disease is suspected, TSH alone can be misleading, so free T4 should always be measured as well.
thinking: Tiredness, cold intolerance, puffiness, heavy periods ↓ Suspected hypothyroidism ↓ No pituitary history ↓ TSH is the most sensitive screen ↓ Add free T4 if abnormal
exam_trap: E, Free T4 on its own — it seems logical to measure the hormone directly, but TSH is more sensitive and picks up early thyroid failure first.
takeaway: TSH is the usual first-line test when primary thyroid dysfunction is suspected.

stem:
A 71-year-old woman has taken oral prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica for over a year. She ran out of tablets five days ago and did not order more. She now presents to her GP feeling extremely weak, nauseated and light-headed, and she nearly fainted getting out of bed.

What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

options.A: Rebound high blood pressure from mineralocorticoid excess
options.B: Worsening hyperglycaemia from loss of insulin sensitivity
options.C: Adrenal insufficiency due to suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
options.D: Acute hypothyroidism from suppression of TSH
options.E: Cushing's syndrome caused by a rebound rise in cortisol

correct_answer: C. Adrenal insufficiency due to suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
why_correct: Months of exogenous glucocorticoid suppress ACTH release, so her adrenal glands have atrophied and cannot produce enough cortisol when the prednisolone stops suddenly. Weakness, nausea and postural light-headedness are typical of secondary adrenal insufficiency, which can progress to crisis. Long-term steroids should be withdrawn gradually, and patients should carry a steroid emergency card and be warned not to stop abruptly.
why_wrong: A. Steroid withdrawal causes low, not high, blood pressure. B. Stopping steroids tends to lower glucose, not raise it. D. Steroids can mildly suppress TSH, but this does not cause acute hypothyroidism. E. Cortisol falls after withdrawal; Cushing's syndrome is caused by excess steroid, not its removal.
pearl: Adrenal suppression should be anticipated in anyone taking the equivalent of prednisolone 5 mg or more daily for longer than about four weeks.
thinking: Over a year of prednisolone ↓ Stopped suddenly ↓ Suppressed ACTH and atrophic adrenals ↓ Not enough endogenous cortisol ↓ Adrenal insufficiency
exam_trap: E, Cushing's syndrome from rebound cortisol — steroids and Cushing's are strongly linked in memory, but stopping them removes cortisol rather than adding it.
takeaway: Long-term corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis, so abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal insufficiency; they must be tapered.

stem:
On a busy acute medical take, the nutrition nurse asks the foundation doctor which of the newly admitted people needs the most cautious introduction of feeding, with thiamine cover and daily checks of phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

Which of these patients is most likely to develop refeeding syndrome?

options.A: A 30-year-old man with obesity who began a supervised weight-loss programme a week ago
options.B: A 58-year-old man with alcohol dependence who has eaten almost nothing for two weeks and has lost a lot of weight
options.C: A fit 25-year-old woman who has fasted overnight before an elective hernia repair
options.D: A 40-year-old woman with well-controlled type 2 diabetes admitted with cellulitis
options.E: A 70-year-old man admitted overnight after day-case cataract surgery

correct_answer: B. A 58-year-old man with alcohol dependence who has eaten almost nothing for two weeks and has lost a lot of weight
why_correct: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is restarted after a period of starvation, causing insulin-driven shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. The highest risk lies with people who have had little or no intake for more than a few days alongside significant weight loss, especially with alcohol misuse, which also causes thiamine deficiency. He needs feeding started slowly with thiamine and close electrolyte monitoring, in line with NICE nutrition support guidance.
why_wrong: A. A modest calorie deficit in someone with obesity does not deplete intracellular stores. C. An overnight fast in a well-nourished person carries no meaningful risk. D. Well-controlled diabetes with a short illness is not a risk factor on its own. E. A brief admission after minor surgery does not involve prolonged starvation.
pearl: NICE defines high refeeding risk as one major criterion (such as very low BMI, marked recent unintentional weight loss, little or no intake for more than 10 days, or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding) or two lesser criteria, one of which can be a history of alcohol misuse.
thinking: Who has prolonged poor intake? ↓ Significant weight loss ↓ Alcohol dependence adds thiamine and electrolyte depletion ↓ Feeding will shift electrolytes into cells ↓ Highest refeeding risk
exam_trap: A, The man with obesity on a weight-loss programme — dieting sounds like restricted intake, but he has ample body stores and has not been starved.
takeaway: Refeeding syndrome risk is greatest after prolonged minimal intake with significant weight loss, particularly in alcohol dependence.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected: NICE refeeding risk = one major criterion or two lesser ones (alcohol misuse is a lesser criterion), replacing inaccurate 'fewer criteria needed with alcohol'

stem:
A 31-year-old accountant visits her GP because her periods stopped five months ago, and she has recently noticed milky fluid leaking from both nipples. A pregnancy test is negative, she has never breastfed and she takes no regular medication. She has also noticed reduced libido.

Which endocrine disturbance is most likely?
why_correct: Inappropriate milk production with loss of periods, once pregnancy and breastfeeding have been excluded, strongly suggests excess prolactin. Prolactin suppresses gonadotrophin-releasing hormone, causing amenorrhoea and low libido, while directly stimulating lactation. Serum prolactin should be measured, and if raised without a drug cause, pituitary imaging is needed to look for a prolactinoma.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism can disturb periods but does not cause galactorrhoea. B. PMOS causes irregular cycles with androgen excess, not milk production. C. Cushing's syndrome may cause menstrual disturbance with central weight gain and bruising, not galactorrhoea. D. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes amenorrhoea with menopausal symptoms but not nipple discharge.
pearl: Dopamine-blocking drugs such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide are a common cause of raised prolactin, so always take a careful drug history.
thinking: Amenorrhoea plus galactorrhoea ↓ Not pregnant or breastfeeding ↓ No interfering drugs ↓ Prolactin suppresses GnRH and drives lactation ↓ Hyperprolactinaemia
exam_trap: B, PMOS (formerly PCOS) — it is the most common cause of disturbed periods, but it does not cause milk production.
takeaway: Galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea in a woman who is not pregnant or breastfeeding points to hyperprolactinaemia.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman sees her GP because her periods have come only every two to three months since her mid-teens. She is troubled by oily skin with acne along her jaw and dark coarse hair on her chin and lower abdomen, and she has gained weight over the past year. A urine pregnancy test is negative.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Infrequent periods since adolescence combined with clinical signs of androgen excess (acne and hirsutism) are the typical presentation of PMOS, which was previously called PCOS. Weight gain and insulin resistance are commonly associated. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by tests to exclude other causes such as thyroid disease, raised prolactin and, where suspected, other sources of androgen.
why_wrong: B. A prolactinoma causes amenorrhoea, often with galactorrhoea, but not hirsutism and acne. C. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes menopausal symptoms without androgen excess. D. Turner syndrome presents with short stature and primary amenorrhoea. E. Hypothyroidism may cause menstrual disturbance and weight gain but not hirsutism and acne.
pearl: Women with PMOS have increased cardiometabolic risk and should be offered regular screening for type 2 diabetes and advice on endometrial protection if they rarely have periods.
thinking: Oligomenorrhoea since adolescence ↓ Acne and hirsutism suggest androgen excess ↓ Pregnancy excluded ↓ Weight gain and likely insulin resistance ↓ PMOS (formerly PCOS)
exam_trap: B, Hyperprolactinaemia due to a prolactinoma — it also causes irregular periods, but the androgen excess here points away from prolactin.
takeaway: Irregular periods with signs of androgen excess in a young woman suggest PMOS (formerly PCOS).

stem:
A 44-year-old woman awaiting pituitary surgery for Cushing's disease tells the endocrine nurse that she can no longer lift her arms to hang the washing on the line and needs to push on her knees to get up from a low sofa. Her hands feel strong and she has no numbness.

Which neuromuscular finding is most likely on examination?

options.A: Distal sensory loss in a stocking distribution
options.E: Symmetrical weakness of the proximal limb muscles

correct_answer: E. Symmetrical weakness of the proximal limb muscles
why_correct: Excess cortisol causes muscle protein breakdown and a myopathy that mainly affects the large proximal muscles of the hips and shoulders. This explains her difficulty raising her arms and standing from a low seat while her hand strength remains normal. The weakness usually improves once cortisol levels are brought under control.
why_wrong: A. Stocking sensory loss is a feature of peripheral neuropathy, and she has no numbness. B. Fasciculations with brisk reflexes suggest motor neurone disease. C. A pill-rolling tremor indicates parkinsonism. D. Fatigable ptosis and diplopia suggest myasthenia gravis.
pearl: Long-term high-dose prednisolone causes the same steroid myopathy as endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
thinking: Cushing's disease ↓ Cannot lift arms or rise from a low seat ↓ Hand strength preserved ↓ Cortisol excess causes muscle catabolism ↓ Proximal myopathy
exam_trap: D, Fatigable ptosis and double vision — myasthenia also causes weakness, but it typically affects eye muscles and fatigues with use, which is not the picture here.
takeaway: Cortisol excess causes a symmetrical proximal myopathy.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman on the surgical ward is reviewed the morning after a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease because she has pins and needles in her fingertips. When the nurse inflates a blood pressure cuff on her upper arm, her wrist flexes and her fingers stiffen and extend, and the spasm releases only when the cuff is deflated.

Which clinical sign has been demonstrated?
why_correct: Inflating a cuff above systolic pressure causes ischaemia of the forearm nerves, which in hypocalcaemia triggers carpal spasm with wrist flexion and finger extension. This is Trousseau's sign. After thyroidectomy it most often reflects damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands, and her calcium should be checked urgently.
why_wrong: A. Chvostek's sign is twitching of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped. B. Kernig's sign is resistance to knee extension with the hip flexed, seen in meningism. C. Murphy's sign is arrest of inspiration on palpating the gallbladder. D. Babinski's sign is an extensor plantar response from an upper motor neurone lesion.
pearl: Trousseau's sign is more specific for hypocalcaemia than Chvostek's sign, which can be present in a minority of people with normal calcium.
thinking: Post-thyroidectomy ↓ Peripheral tingling ↓ Cuff inflation induces carpal spasm ↓ Neuromuscular irritability from low calcium ↓ Trousseau's sign
exam_trap: A, Chvostek's sign — both signs indicate hypocalcaemia and are often confused, but Chvostek's involves tapping the face rather than inflating a cuff.
takeaway: Carpal spasm provoked by inflating a blood pressure cuff is Trousseau's sign of hypocalcaemia.

stem:
A 45-year-old man is on day three of an admission for severe acute pancreatitis. He tells the night doctor that his lips feel numb and his hands keep cramping painfully. His adjusted calcium is low.

Which clinical feature on examination would be most in keeping with his electrolyte disturbance?

options.E: Reduced tendon reflexes with floppy muscles

why_correct: Low calcium lowers the threshold for nerve depolarisation, making nerves and muscles excitable. This produces perioral and peripheral paraesthesia, muscle cramps and tetany, with carpopedal spasm. Acute pancreatitis causes hypocalcaemia through saponification of calcium in the inflamed fatty tissue.
why_wrong: B. Polyuria and thirst are features of high calcium. C. Renal stones are linked to hypercalcaemia, such as in primary hyperparathyroidism. D. Clubbing is not caused by any calcium disturbance. E. Hyporeflexia and hypotonia are seen with high calcium, while low calcium causes brisk reflexes.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia in acute pancreatitis is one of the markers of disease severity in scoring systems such as the Glasgow criteria.
thinking: Severe acute pancreatitis ↓ Perioral numbness and hand cramps ↓ Adjusted calcium low ↓ Increased neuromuscular excitability ↓ Tetany
exam_trap: C, Recurrent renal colic from stones — calcium and kidney stones are closely linked, but stones belong to hypercalcaemia, not a low calcium.
takeaway: Hypocalcaemia causes neuromuscular irritability, with paraesthesia, cramps and tetany.

presentation: Red flag features of a thyroid lump
stem:
A 67-year-old man sees his GP after his wife noticed a swelling at the front of his neck. On examination there is a firm lump in the right lobe of the thyroid. The GP considers which features in the history would most increase the likelihood of thyroid cancer.

Which feature is the most concerning?

options.A: The lump moves upwards when he swallows
options.B: He has a sister with hypothyroidism
options.C: He has had a mild cold recently
options.D: The lump was slightly tender after a sore throat
options.E: The lump has grown noticeably over a few weeks

correct_answer: E. The lump has grown noticeably over a few weeks
why_correct: Rapid growth of a thyroid mass over weeks is a red flag for malignancy, including aggressive tumours such as anaplastic carcinoma or lymphoma. Together with features such as hoarseness, stridor, a hard fixed lump or cervical lymphadenopathy, it needs urgent assessment through a suspected cancer pathway.
why_wrong: A. All thyroid swellings move on swallowing, so this only confirms the lump is thyroid. B. A family history of hypothyroidism does not raise cancer risk. C. A recent cold is irrelevant. D. Tenderness after a viral illness suggests subacute thyroiditis, which is benign.
pearl: Unexplained hoarseness or stridor with a thyroid lump suggests local invasion, such as recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, and needs very urgent assessment.
thinking: Thyroid lump in an older man ↓ Which feature points to malignancy? ↓ Movement on swallowing only localises ↓ Rapid growth suggests aggressive disease ↓ Urgent cancer assessment
exam_trap: A, The lump moves on swallowing — this is a well-known examination finding for neck lumps, but it simply shows the lump is in the thyroid and says nothing about malignancy.
takeaway: Rapid enlargement of a thyroid lump is a red flag for malignancy and needs urgent assessment.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman sees her GP with a year of slowly increasing tiredness, weight gain and constipation. Her neck has become fuller, and examination finds a firm, rubbery, non-tender diffuse goitre. Blood tests show a raised TSH and a low free T4. She lives in the UK and eats a normal diet.

What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A firm, diffuse, painless goitre with gradually developing primary hypothyroidism is the typical presentation of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the gland causes the goitre and progressive loss of thyroid hormone production. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are usually strongly positive, and treatment is with levothyroxine.
why_wrong: A. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism, not low free T4. B. De Quervain thyroiditis causes a painful tender gland after a viral illness, usually with an initial thyrotoxic phase. C. Toxic multinodular goitre causes hyperthyroidism with a nodular gland. E. Iodine deficiency is the commonest cause worldwide but rare in the UK with a normal diet.
pearl: Hashimoto thyroiditis carries a small increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma, so a rapidly enlarging goitre in a patient with this condition needs urgent assessment.
thinking: Gradual hypothyroid symptoms ↓ Firm, rubbery, painless diffuse goitre ↓ High TSH with low free T4 ↓ Iodine-sufficient UK setting ↓ Autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis
exam_trap: A, Graves disease — it is the best known autoimmune thyroid disease with a diffuse goitre, but it causes an overactive gland rather than hypothyroidism.
takeaway: In iodine-sufficient countries, Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism with a goitre.

presentation: Initial investigation of a thyroid nodule
stem:
A 39-year-old man attends his GP after noticing a painless lump low in his neck while shaving. Examination reveals a single discrete nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid that moves on swallowing. He has no hoarseness, swallowing difficulty or breathlessness, and there are no palpable lymph nodes. No blood tests have been done yet.

Which investigation should be carried out first?
why_correct: Thyroid function, starting with TSH, is the first test for any thyroid nodule because the result determines what follows. A suppressed TSH suggests a hyperfunctioning nodule, which is very rarely malignant and is assessed with an uptake scan, whereas a normal or raised TSH leads on to ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration if the appearance is suspicious, in line with NICE guidance on thyroid disease.
why_wrong: A. Fine-needle aspiration is guided by ultrasound features and is not the first step. B. An uptake scan is only useful if the TSH is suppressed. D. CT is not a first-line test and is reserved for assessing large or retrosternal goitres. E. Calcitonin is not part of routine first-line assessment of a nodule.
pearl: Ultrasound is the key imaging test for thyroid nodules and grades them using a risk classification (such as U1 to U5) to decide which need cytology.
thinking: Single thyroid nodule ↓ No compressive or red-flag symptoms ↓ Function determines the pathway ↓ Check TSH first ↓ Then ultrasound or uptake scan accordingly
exam_trap: A, Fine-needle aspiration cytology — the main worry is cancer, so going straight to cytology is tempting, but sampling is guided by TSH and ultrasound findings first.
takeaway: The first investigation for a thyroid nodule is a serum TSH, which determines the next step.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with palpitations. Over the past two months she has lost weight despite a good appetite, feels hot when others are comfortable, and has a fine tremor of her outstretched hands. Her ECG shows atrial fibrillation, which has not been recorded before.

Which underlying endocrine disorder should be tested for?
why_correct: Weight loss despite a good appetite, heat intolerance and a fine tremor are classic features of thyrotoxicosis, which increases sympathetic sensitivity and is a recognised cause of new atrial fibrillation, particularly in older people. Thyroid function should be checked in all patients presenting with new atrial fibrillation, and treating the hyperthyroidism often helps restore sinus rhythm.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia. C. Addison disease causes weight loss but with fatigue, pigmentation and hypotension rather than heat intolerance and tremor. D. Hyperparathyroidism causes thirst, constipation and bone pain rather than this picture. E. Cushing syndrome causes weight gain and central obesity.
pearl: Older people with hyperthyroidism may have few classic symptoms (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), so atrial fibrillation or weight loss may be the only clue.
thinking: New atrial fibrillation ↓ Weight loss with good appetite ↓ Heat intolerance and fine tremor ↓ Excess thyroid hormone ↓ Hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: A, Hypothyroidism — both thyroid states disturb the heart, but underactivity slows the rate, whereas weight loss and heat intolerance point to overactivity.
takeaway: Check thyroid function in new atrial fibrillation, as hyperthyroidism is a reversible cause.

stem:
At the endocrine clinic, a 58-year-old man is reviewed after his GP found a suppressed TSH with a raised free T4. He has lost weight and feels jittery, and examination reveals a single firm lump in the left lobe of his thyroid. There are no eye signs. The team want to know whether this lump is the source of his excess hormone.

Which imaging test would best answer this?

options.C: Technetium or radioiodine thyroid uptake scan
options.D: Chest X-ray including the thoracic inlet
options.E: PET-CT of the neck and chest

correct_answer: C. Technetium or radioiodine thyroid uptake scan
why_correct: In a patient who is thyrotoxic with a nodule, the key question is whether the nodule itself is producing hormone. A radionuclide (technetium-99m pertechnetate or radioiodine) scan shows uptake, so a toxic adenoma appears as a 'hot' nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland. Hot nodules are very rarely malignant, which also guides whether further cytology is needed.
why_wrong: A. CT gives anatomical detail only, and iodinated contrast can block thyroid uptake for weeks and delay radionuclide imaging or radioiodine treatment. B. MRI shows structure, not iodine uptake, so it cannot tell whether the lump is functioning. D. A chest film may show tracheal deviation or retrosternal extension but says nothing about function. E. PET-CT is not used to assess thyroid nodule function, and incidental thyroid uptake on PET needs separate work-up.
pearl: A hot nodule on uptake scanning is almost always benign, whereas a cold nodule needs ultrasound-guided assessment for malignancy.
thinking: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 ↓ Single palpable thyroid nodule ↓ Question is whether the nodule is autonomous ↓ Function is shown by isotope uptake, not anatomy ↓ Radionuclide uptake scan
exam_trap: A, Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck — it sounds like thorough imaging, but it shows anatomy only and the iodine load can interfere with later isotope scanning and radioiodine therapy.
takeaway: To find out whether a thyroid nodule is overproducing hormone, use a radionuclide uptake scan.

stem:
Clare, a 39-year-old teacher, felt a painless lump to the right of her windpipe while applying moisturiser. At her GP appointment the lump moves on swallowing, there are no enlarged nodes and she has no symptoms of an over- or underactive thyroid. No thyroid bloods have yet been taken.

Which blood test should be requested first?
why_correct: TSH is the first blood test for anyone with a new thyroid lump because it decides the next step. A low TSH points to a possible hot (functioning) nodule, which is then assessed with isotope scanning, while a normal or raised TSH leads on to ultrasound assessment. The other tests are not part of routine first-line work-up.
why_wrong: A. Thyroglobulin is used to monitor for recurrence after thyroid cancer treatment, not to assess a new nodule. C. Calcitonin is reserved for suspected medullary carcinoma or MEN 2 and is not a routine first test. D. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies help with autoimmune thyroid disease but do not direct nodule assessment. E. Calcium is relevant to parathyroid disease, not to the work-up of a thyroid lump.
pearl: Thyroglobulin is a tumour marker for follow-up after total thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer, not a diagnostic test.
thinking: New lump moving with swallowing ↓ Thyroid origin likely ↓ Need to know thyroid function before choosing imaging ↓ Low TSH suggests a functioning nodule; normal TSH leads to ultrasound ↓ TSH first
exam_trap: A, Thyroglobulin — it is a thyroid-specific protein and sounds like a cancer screen, but it cannot distinguish benign from malignant nodules and is only useful after treatment.
takeaway: Check TSH first in any new thyroid nodule because the result decides the next investigation.

stem:
A 41-year-old man attends his GP because his family have noticed a fullness at the front of his neck. Over the last two months he has felt restless and has been sleeping poorly. His TSH is undetectable and the GP wants to check for other features of thyrotoxicosis.

Which additional symptom would be most in keeping with this?

options.A: Feeling cold in a warm room
options.D: Preferring cool rooms and sweating easily

correct_answer: D. Preferring cool rooms and sweating easily
why_correct: Excess thyroid hormone increases the metabolic rate and heat production, so patients dislike warm environments and sweat more. This fits with his undetectable TSH and restlessness. The other options describe a slowed metabolism and point towards hypothyroidism.
why_wrong: A. Feeling cold is typical of hypothyroidism. B. A slow pulse fits hypothyroidism; thyrotoxicosis causes tachycardia. C. Constipation is a hypothyroid feature; thyrotoxicosis tends to cause frequent loose stools. E. Weight gain suggests hypothyroidism, whereas thyrotoxicosis usually causes weight loss despite a good appetite.
pearl: Thyrotoxicosis usually causes weight loss with increased appetite, but some younger patients gain weight because appetite rises more than energy use.
thinking: Neck swelling with restlessness ↓ Undetectable TSH suggests thyrotoxicosis ↓ Raised metabolic rate increases heat production ↓ Heat intolerance and sweating fit ↓ Cold intolerance, bradycardia and constipation suggest the opposite state
exam_trap: A, Feeling cold in a warm room — temperature intolerance is a classic thyroid symptom, but cold intolerance belongs to hypothyroidism, not thyrotoxicosis.
takeaway: Heat intolerance and sweating point to an overactive thyroid.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman tells the practice nurse that for several weeks she has noticed white, milk-like fluid leaking from both nipples and staining her bra. Her youngest child is eight and she has not breastfed for years. There is no breast lump, redness or pain.

What is the correct medical term for her symptom?
why_correct: Galactorrhoea is the production or discharge of milk from the breast unrelated to pregnancy or breastfeeding. Bilateral milky discharge from several ducts is typical. It should prompt a pregnancy test, a medication review and a serum prolactin.
why_wrong: A. Mastalgia means breast pain, which she does not have. B. Duct ectasia causes thick, often green or cream discharge, usually from one nipple, in older women, and is a structural condition rather than milk production. D. Gynaecomastia is enlargement of male breast tissue. E. Mastitis is inflammation of the breast with pain, redness and warmth.
pearl: Common drug causes of galactorrhoea include antipsychotics such as risperidone and dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide and domperidone.
thinking: Bilateral milky nipple discharge ↓ Not pregnant and not breastfeeding ↓ No inflammation or lump ↓ Inappropriate milk production ↓ Galactorrhoea
exam_trap: B, Duct ectasia — it is a recognised cause of nipple discharge, but the discharge is thick and coloured from dilated ducts, not milk.
takeaway: Milk discharge outside pregnancy and breastfeeding is called galactorrhoea.

stem:
Over the last year, the periods of a 31-year-old woman have become sparse and she now goes several months between them. She has also noticed a milky fluid when she squeezes her nipples. A pregnancy test is negative, she takes no regular medicines and her thyroid function is normal. She is seen in the gynaecology clinic.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Galactorrhoea combined with oligomenorrhoea suggests hyperprolactinaemia, because prolactin both stimulates milk production and suppresses GnRH, reducing ovulation. With pregnancy, drugs and hypothyroidism excluded, a prolactinoma is the most likely cause. A serum prolactin followed by pituitary MRI would confirm it.
why_wrong: A. Cushing syndrome causes menstrual upset but with central weight gain, striae and bruising rather than milk discharge. C. Primary ovarian insufficiency causes amenorrhoea with menopausal symptoms, not galactorrhoea. D. Acromegaly causes enlargement of hands, feet and facial features; galactorrhoea is uncommon. E. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes irregular cycles with hirsutism or acne, and any prolactin rise is mild.
pearl: Hypothyroidism can cause hyperprolactinaemia because raised TRH stimulates prolactin release, so always check thyroid function.
thinking: Milky nipple discharge ↓ Infrequent periods ↓ Pregnancy, drugs and hypothyroidism excluded ↓ Raised prolactin suppresses GnRH and drives lactation ↓ Prolactinoma
exam_trap: E, Polycystic ovary syndrome — it is the commonest cause of irregular periods in young women, but it does not explain true galactorrhoea.
takeaway: Galactorrhoea with oligomenorrhoea, once pregnancy, drugs and hypothyroidism are excluded, suggests a prolactinoma.

stem:
At his annual diabetes review, a 71-year-old retired builder who has had type 2 diabetes for twenty years mentions that he recently found a drawing pin stuck in his heel that he had not felt. On testing, he cannot feel a 10 g monofilament at several points on the soles of either foot and vibration sense is lost at both big toes. Foot pulses are easily palpable.

Which complication best explains his findings?
why_correct: Symmetrical, stocking-distribution loss of protective sensation and vibration sense in a man with long-standing diabetes is diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy. Damage to the longest nerve fibres first explains why the feet are affected and why injuries go unnoticed. His palpable pulses argue against an ischaemic cause.
why_wrong: A. Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication with leg pain on walking, not fixed symmetrical loss of protective sensation. B. Peripheral arterial disease causes claudication, absent pulses and poor healing, and his pulses are normal. D. Charcot foot is a complication of neuropathy causing a hot, swollen, deformed foot, not the cause of sensory loss. E. Radiculopathy follows a dermatomal pattern with back pain and is rarely symmetrical.
pearl: Loss of sensation to a 10 g monofilament marks loss of protective sensation and places the foot at increased risk of ulceration.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ Unnoticed foot injury ↓ Symmetrical loss of monofilament and vibration sense ↓ Pulses present so not ischaemic ↓ Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy
exam_trap: D, Charcot neuroarthropathy — it is a diabetic foot complication, but it results from neuropathy and presents as a hot swollen foot rather than explaining the sensory loss.
takeaway: Symmetrical distal sensory loss in long-standing diabetes is peripheral neuropathy until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is told at her podiatry assessment that she has lost protective sensation in both feet, though there is no ulcer and her pulses are present. She asks what she can do herself to avoid problems.

Which advice is most important to reduce her risk of foot ulceration?

options.A: Soak both feet in a hot bath each night to soften the skin
options.B: Pare down hard skin at home with a razor blade
options.C: Go barefoot indoors to strengthen the skin
options.D: Use medicated corn plasters on any thickened areas
options.E: Inspect her feet every day and wear well-fitting protective footwear

correct_answer: E. Inspect her feet every day and wear well-fitting protective footwear
why_correct: Without protective sensation, small injuries go unnoticed and progress to ulcers. Daily self-inspection (using a mirror or a relative if needed), well-fitting shoes and socks, and regular review by the foot protection service are the mainstay of prevention recommended by NICE. Any new wound or colour change should be reported promptly.
why_wrong: A. Hot water can burn numb skin without her noticing, and prolonged soaking macerates the skin. B. Cutting hard skin at home risks cuts and infection; this should be done by a podiatrist. C. Walking barefoot exposes insensate feet to unnoticed trauma. D. Medicated corn plasters contain salicylic acid, which can cause chemical ulceration in a diabetic foot.
pearl: NICE advises that people with diabetes at increased risk of foot problems are referred to the foot protection service, and that active ulceration or infection is referred urgently to the multidisciplinary foot care service.
thinking: Loss of protective sensation ↓ Injuries will not be felt ↓ Prevention depends on spotting damage early and avoiding trauma ↓ Daily inspection and protective footwear ↓ Avoid heat, sharp instruments and acid plasters
exam_trap: D, Use medicated corn plasters on any thickened areas — they are sold over the counter for hard skin, but the acid can ulcerate numb diabetic skin.
takeaway: People with diabetic neuropathy should check their feet daily and wear protective, well-fitting footwear.

stem:
A 37-year-old woman with newly confirmed Graves disease phones the endocrine nurse helpline. She has started carbimazole but says her hands shake so much she cannot write and her heart races at night. She has no asthma and no heart failure. Her consultant has said full control of her thyroid will take several weeks.

Which medicine is most appropriate to ease these symptoms in the meantime?
why_correct: Many symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, including tremor, palpitations, sweating and anxiety, are driven by increased sensitivity to adrenergic stimulation. A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol relieves these quickly while antithyroid drugs take several weeks to lower hormone levels. It is contraindicated in asthma, which she does not have.
why_wrong: A. Diazepam may reduce anxiety but does not treat the adrenergic tremor and tachycardia, and carries a dependence risk. B. Levothyroxine is thyroid hormone replacement and would worsen thyrotoxicosis unless used in a block-and-replace regimen. C. Digoxin is used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, but she has a sinus tachycardia and digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxic states. D. Amlodipine lowers blood pressure but does not control tremor or heart rate.
pearl: Rate-limiting calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem are an alternative for symptom control when beta-blockers are contraindicated.
thinking: New Graves disease on carbimazole ↓ Antithyroid drugs act slowly ↓ Tremor and palpitations are adrenergic ↓ No asthma so beta-blockade is safe ↓ Propranolol
exam_trap: C, Digoxin — it slows the heart in atrial fibrillation, but she has adrenergic sinus tachycardia and tremor, which a beta-blocker treats far better.
takeaway: Use a beta-blocker such as propranolol for adrenergic symptoms while waiting for antithyroid treatment to work.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because she has felt her heart fluttering for two days. She has lost weight over the summer and has a fine tremor and warm, moist skin. Her pulse is irregularly irregular. Blood tests sent from triage show an undetectable TSH.

Which cardiac complication is most likely to explain her presentation?
why_correct: Thyroid hormone increases sympathetic tone and atrial excitability, making atrial fibrillation the commonest arrhythmia in thyrotoxicosis. Older people may present with AF and weight loss with few classic symptoms, so thyroid function should be checked in all new AF. An irregularly irregular pulse in this context fits AF.
why_wrong: A. Complete heart block causes a slow regular pulse and is not a feature of thyrotoxicosis. B. Constrictive pericarditis causes raised venous pressure and oedema, not a thyroid-driven arrhythmia. D. Mitral stenosis can cause AF but is a valve disease with no link to her thyroid results. E. Ventricular tachycardia is usually regular and is not the typical thyrotoxic arrhythmia.
pearl: In thyrotoxic AF, beta-blockers are the mainstay of rate control, and the need for anticoagulation is assessed in the usual way using stroke risk.
thinking: Older woman with weight loss and tremor ↓ Undetectable TSH confirms thyrotoxicosis ↓ Irregularly irregular pulse ↓ Thyroid hormone excess predisposes to atrial arrhythmia ↓ Atrial fibrillation
exam_trap: D, Mitral stenosis — it classically causes atrial fibrillation, but nothing here suggests valve disease and her thyroid results give the explanation.
takeaway: Thyrotoxicosis commonly causes atrial fibrillation, especially in older people, so check thyroid function in new AF.

stem:
A 26-year-old graphic designer sees her GP because for about six weeks she has felt shaky, sweats even in cool weather and notices her heart pounding. She has lost weight while eating more and her periods have become lighter. Her resting pulse is fast and regular every time it is checked, and she has a fine tremor of her outstretched hands.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Weight loss despite a bigger appetite, heat intolerance with sweating, a persistent resting tachycardia, fine tremor and lighter periods together indicate excess thyroid hormone. The symptoms are continuous rather than episodic, which points away from paroxysmal causes. Thyroid function tests would confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety can cause palpitations and tremor but not weight loss with increased appetite and a persistently fast resting pulse. C. Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal attacks of headache, sweating and hypertension rather than continuous symptoms. D. Hypothyroidism causes a slow pulse, weight gain and cold intolerance. E. Insulinoma causes episodic fasting hypoglycaemia relieved by eating, usually with weight gain.
pearl: Check thyroid function before diagnosing an anxiety disorder in someone with palpitations, tremor and weight loss.
thinking: Continuous rather than episodic symptoms ↓ Sweating, tremor, tachycardia ↓ Weight loss with increased appetite ↓ Lighter periods ↓ Hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: A, Generalised anxiety disorder — tremor and palpitations overlap, but weight loss with a raised appetite and persistent tachycardia point to a thyroid cause.
takeaway: Persistent tachycardia, tremor, sweating and weight loss with a good appetite suggest hyperthyroidism.

stem:
A 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes rings NHS 111 from his flat. He took his usual insulin but missed lunch, and now feels sweaty and shaky. He is talking clearly and can swallow, and his meter reads below 4 mmol/L. He asks what to do straight away.

What is the most appropriate immediate advice?

options.A: Take a fast-acting sugary drink or glucose tablets now, then recheck in 15 minutes
options.B: Give himself an extra dose of rapid-acting insulin
options.C: Lie down and rest until the symptoms settle
options.D: Drink a large glass of water and wait
options.E: Eat a portion of wholegrain bread only

correct_answer: A. Take a fast-acting sugary drink or glucose tablets now, then recheck in 15 minutes
why_correct: He has mild hypoglycaemia and is conscious and able to swallow, so the immediate treatment is quick-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink. The glucose should be rechecked after about 15 minutes and treatment repeated if it is still low. Once recovered, a longer-acting carbohydrate snack or his next meal helps prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: B. Extra insulin would lower his glucose further and could cause dangerous hypoglycaemia. C. Resting without treatment allows hypoglycaemia to progress to confusion or loss of consciousness. D. Water contains no glucose and will not correct hypoglycaemia. E. Wholegrain bread is slowly absorbed; it is useful after initial correction but is too slow as first treatment.
pearl: Glucagon or intravenous glucose is reserved for hypoglycaemia when the person cannot safely swallow; oral treatment is used whenever swallowing is safe.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes on insulin with a missed meal ↓ Sweaty, shaky, low meter reading ↓ Conscious and able to swallow ↓ Give quick-acting oral carbohydrate ↓ Recheck after 15 minutes then follow with longer-acting carbohydrate
exam_trap: E, Eat a portion of wholegrain bread only — it is sensible follow-up, but slowly absorbed carbohydrate is too slow to correct hypoglycaemia on its own.
takeaway: Treat conscious hypoglycaemia with fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes and follow with a longer-acting snack.

stem:
On the morning after surgery for Graves disease in which her whole thyroid was removed, a 45-year-old woman on the surgical ward complains that her lips and fingertips feel like pins and needles. While the nurse is taking her blood pressure, her hand cramps into flexion at the wrist and knuckles with the fingers held straight and the thumb drawn in.

Which blood result is most likely to be abnormal?
why_correct: Total thyroidectomy can damage the parathyroid glands or their blood supply, causing a sudden fall in parathyroid hormone and hence serum calcium. Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, producing perioral and fingertip paraesthesia and carpal spasm when the cuff is inflated (Trousseau sign). This needs prompt measurement of calcium and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Hyperkalaemia causes weakness and ECG changes, not paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm. B. Hyponatraemia causes confusion, headache and seizures rather than tetany. C. Raised calcium causes thirst, constipation and confusion, the opposite of tetany. D. Hyperglycaemia does not cause tetany.
pearl: Hypomagnesaemia impairs parathyroid hormone secretion and action, so magnesium should be checked and corrected in persistent hypocalcaemia.
thinking: Day after total thyroidectomy ↓ Perioral and fingertip tingling ↓ Carpal spasm with the cuff (Trousseau sign) ↓ Parathyroid injury lowers PTH ↓ Low calcium
exam_trap: C, Raised calcium — a calcium disturbance is right in principle, but high calcium causes thirst and constipation, not tetany after neck surgery.
takeaway: Tingling and carpopedal spasm after total thyroidectomy indicate hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem: corrected description of Trousseau carpal spasm (flexion at wrist and MCP joints, straight fingers, adducted thumb)

stem:
A 48-year-old man is investigated on the endocrine ward for passing large volumes of pale urine, with normal blood glucose and calcium. During a supervised water deprivation test his urine stays dilute despite rising plasma osmolality. After a dose of desmopressin, his urine osmolality rises sharply.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: E. Cranial diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency)
why_correct: Failure to concentrate urine during water deprivation shows a problem with ADH, and a marked rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin shows the kidneys respond normally. The defect is therefore lack of ADH production or release from the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary. This is cranial diabetes insipidus, now termed arginine vasopressin deficiency.
why_wrong: A. In primary polydipsia the urine concentrates during water deprivation because ADH secretion is intact. B. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the kidneys do not respond, so desmopressin produces little change. C. SIADH causes concentrated urine with hyponatraemia, not dilute polyuria. D. Osmotic diuresis needs a solute such as glucose, and his glucose is normal.
pearl: Once cranial diabetes insipidus is confirmed, pituitary MRI is needed to look for a structural cause such as a tumour or infiltrative disease.
thinking: Dilute polyuria with normal glucose and calcium ↓ Urine stays dilute during water deprivation ↓ Desmopressin markedly concentrates urine ↓ Kidneys respond, so ADH is missing ↓ Cranial diabetes insipidus
exam_trap: B, Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — it causes the same dilute polyuria, but the kidneys would not respond to desmopressin.
takeaway: A clear rise in urine concentration after desmopressin indicates cranial rather than nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with bipolar disorder who has taken lithium for many years is seen by his community mental health team. He is getting up four times a night to pass urine and keeps large bottles of water by his bed. His blood glucose and calcium are normal and his lithium level is within range. Tests show his urine stays dilute even when he is dehydrated, and desmopressin makes little difference.

Which mechanism best explains his symptoms?

options.B: Reduced response of the renal collecting ducts to ADH
options.C: Failure of ADH release from the posterior pituitary
options.D: Osmotic diuresis from glucose in the urine
options.E: Compulsive water drinking with normal ADH function

correct_answer: B. Reduced response of the renal collecting ducts to ADH
why_correct: Long-term lithium accumulates in collecting duct cells and reduces aquaporin-2 expression, so the kidney cannot respond to ADH. This produces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with persistently dilute urine. The lack of response to desmopressin confirms the problem is renal rather than pituitary.
why_wrong: A. Excess cortisol causes Cushing features and is not related to lithium. C. Pituitary ADH deficiency would respond to desmopressin. D. His glucose is normal, so there is no glycosuria to cause osmotic diuresis. E. In primary polydipsia the urine concentrates when dehydrated because ADH release and renal response are intact.
pearl: Lithium also causes hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia, so thyroid function, calcium and renal function are monitored alongside lithium levels.
thinking: Long-term lithium ↓ Nocturia and thirst ↓ Normal glucose and calcium ↓ Urine stays dilute when dehydrated with no desmopressin response ↓ Renal resistance to ADH
exam_trap: C, Failure of ADH release from the posterior pituitary — it also causes dilute polyuria, but desmopressin would correct it and lithium acts on the kidney.
takeaway: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by making the collecting ducts resistant to ADH.

stem:
Over the past month a 15-year-old girl's trousers have become loose, she is up repeatedly at night to pass urine and she carries a water bottle everywhere. Her mother brings her to the GP, where a fingerprick glucose is high and her urine shows ketones. She is slim and has no family history of diabetes.

What is the underlying cause of her condition?

options.A: Resistance of peripheral tissues to insulin
options.B: Immune-mediated destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic cells
options.C: Overproduction of glucagon by a pancreatic tumour
options.D: Failure of ADH release from the pituitary
options.E: Excess cortisol production by the adrenal glands

correct_answer: B. Immune-mediated destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic cells
why_correct: Rapid weight loss, thirst and polyuria with hyperglycaemia and ketonuria in a slim teenager indicate type 1 diabetes. This results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency. Without insulin, fat is broken down to ketones, which is why ketonuria is present, and she needs same-day specialist referral.
why_wrong: A. Insulin resistance underlies type 2 diabetes, usually in older or overweight people without early ketosis. C. A glucagonoma is very rare and causes a characteristic rash with weight loss in adults. D. ADH deficiency causes dilute polyuria with normal glucose. E. Excess cortisol causes central weight gain, not rapid weight loss.
pearl: Suspected type 1 diabetes in a child or young person should be referred the same day to a paediatric diabetes team because of the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.
thinking: Slim teenager ↓ Weight loss, thirst and nocturia over weeks ↓ Hyperglycaemia with ketonuria ↓ Absolute insulin deficiency ↓ Autoimmune beta-cell destruction
exam_trap: A, Resistance of peripheral tissues to insulin — it explains type 2 diabetes, but ketosis and weight loss in a slim teenager point to absolute insulin deficiency.
takeaway: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells.

stem:
A 30-year-old man with confirmed diabetes insipidus is reviewed on the medical ward. He passes many litres of urine a day and drinks constantly to keep up. His blood glucose and calcium are normal. The ward doctor explains to a newly qualified nurse what his urine will typically show at the bedside.

Which finding is characteristic?

options.A: Large amount of glucose on dipstick
options.D: Very dilute urine with low osmolality

correct_answer: D. Very dilute urine with low osmolality
why_correct: In diabetes insipidus, ADH is either lacking or ineffective, so the collecting ducts cannot reabsorb water. The result is large volumes of pale urine with low specific gravity and low osmolality, even when the body is dehydrated. This contrasts with diabetes mellitus, where glycosuria drives the polyuria.
why_wrong: A. Glycosuria is the cause of polyuria in diabetes mellitus, not diabetes insipidus. B. Heavy proteinuria suggests glomerular disease. C. Haematuria suggests a urological or renal cause and is not part of diabetes insipidus. E. Concentrated urine would indicate normal ADH action, the opposite of diabetes insipidus.
pearl: A water deprivation test followed by desmopressin distinguishes cranial from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and both from primary polydipsia.
thinking: Large urine volumes and thirst ↓ Normal glucose and calcium ↓ ADH absent or ineffective ↓ Water cannot be reabsorbed ↓ Very dilute urine
exam_trap: A, Large amount of glucose on dipstick — the word diabetes invites this, but glycosuria belongs to diabetes mellitus.
takeaway: Diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of very dilute urine.

stem:
Two days after transsphenoidal removal of a pituitary adenoma, a 54-year-old man on the neurosurgical ward is passing large volumes of pale urine and repeatedly asking for water. His urine osmolality is low and his serum sodium has risen towards the top of the range. His glucose is normal.

Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Pituitary surgery can damage the posterior pituitary or pituitary stalk, disrupting ADH release. Polyuria with dilute urine, thirst and a rising sodium indicate diabetes insipidus. It may be transient or permanent and is treated with desmopressin and careful fluid balance.
why_wrong: A. SIADH also occurs after pituitary surgery but causes concentrated urine with hyponatraemia. B. Cerebral salt wasting causes hyponatraemia with volume depletion and salt-rich urine. C. Adrenal insufficiency causes hypotension and hyponatraemia rather than dilute polyuria with rising sodium. D. His glucose is normal, so there is no osmotic diuresis.
pearl: After pituitary surgery, sodium can follow a triphasic pattern of diabetes insipidus, then SIADH, then sometimes permanent diabetes insipidus, so fluid balance and sodium are monitored closely.
thinking: Recent pituitary surgery ↓ Large volumes of pale urine and thirst ↓ Low urine osmolality with rising sodium ↓ Normal glucose ↓ Diabetes insipidus
exam_trap: A, Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion — it is also a recognised complication of pituitary surgery, but it causes concentrated urine and low sodium.
takeaway: Dilute polyuria with rising sodium after pituitary surgery suggests diabetes insipidus.

stem:
A 61-year-old taxi driver attends a health check because he is always tired and is having to stop for the toilet several times during his shifts. He is also drinking far more than usual and has had two episodes of thrush. He is overweight. His fasting glucose and HbA1c are both raised on repeat testing.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Thirst, polyuria, tiredness and recurrent thrush with repeatedly raised glucose and HbA1c confirm diabetes mellitus, most likely type 2 in an overweight older man. Glycosuria causes an osmotic diuresis and thirst and promotes candida infection. Persistently abnormal results in someone with symptoms confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong: B. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute polyuria with normal glucose. C. Hyperparathyroidism can cause thirst and polyuria through hypercalcaemia but would not raise glucose or HbA1c. D. Hypothyroidism causes tiredness and weight gain but not thirst or polyuria. E. Chronic kidney disease can cause nocturia but does not raise glucose and HbA1c.
pearl: Drivers treated with insulin or sulfonylureas must follow DVLA rules on glucose monitoring and hypoglycaemia awareness.
thinking: Thirst and polyuria ↓ Tiredness and recurrent thrush ↓ Raised fasting glucose and HbA1c on repeat ↓ Overweight older adult ↓ Diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: B, Diabetes insipidus — it shares thirst and polyuria, but glucose is normal and the urine is dilute rather than glucose-laden.
takeaway: Polyuria and thirst with persistently raised glucose and HbA1c indicate diabetes mellitus.

presentation: Cranial diabetes insipidus after head trauma
stem:
Ten days after being admitted to the neurosurgical ward following a fall from scaffolding with a basal skull fracture, a 46-year-old roofer is drinking jug after jug of water and his fluid balance chart shows several litres of pale urine a day. His capillary glucose is normal and his plasma sodium is drifting upwards.

Which condition best explains this?
why_correct: Trauma to the skull base can injure the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary, so too little ADH is released. The kidneys cannot concentrate urine, producing large volumes of dilute urine and compensatory thirst, with sodium creeping up when intake does not keep pace. Normal glucose excludes an osmotic diuresis.
why_wrong: A. Primary polydipsia causes dilution with a low or low-normal sodium, not a rising sodium. B. SIADH causes concentrated urine, fluid retention and hyponatraemia, the opposite picture. D. Nephrogenic DI is due to renal ADH resistance (for example lithium or hypercalcaemia), not head injury. E. HHS requires marked hyperglycaemia, and his glucose is normal.
pearl: Cranial DI responds to desmopressin with a rise in urine osmolality, whereas nephrogenic DI does not; a water deprivation test with desmopressin separates the two.
thinking: Recent basal skull fracture ↓ Polyuria of dilute urine with intense thirst ↓ Glucose normal, so no osmotic diuresis ↓ Sodium rising suggests water loss rather than excess intake ↓ Damage to the hypothalamic-pituitary axis means ADH deficiency
exam_trap: D, Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — it produces an identical urine picture, but the cause lies in the kidney (drugs, electrolytes), whereas head trauma points to failure of ADH release.
takeaway: Dilute polyuria with rising sodium after head injury suggests cranial diabetes insipidus.

stem:
Over the past few months, a 57-year-old taxi driver has noticed he is passing urine more often and keeps a bottle of water in his cab. He has a BMI in the obese range, his mother developed diabetes in her sixties, and he has had two episodes of balanitis. Two HbA1c results taken a fortnight apart are both clearly in the diabetic range. Urine ketones are negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradual osmotic symptoms, recurrent genital candidal infection, obesity and a family history in a middle-aged adult, with two diagnostic HbA1c results and no ketosis, fit type 2 diabetes. Two abnormal results confirm the diagnosis in someone without acute hyperglycaemic illness.
why_wrong: B. Type 1 diabetes usually presents more abruptly in a younger, slimmer person with weight loss and ketones. C. Diabetes insipidus does not raise HbA1c. D. Hyperparathyroidism can cause thirst and polyuria but not hyperglycaemia or balanitis. E. Cushing syndrome can cause hyperglycaemia but needs features such as proximal myopathy, striae and easy bruising, which are absent.
pearl: A single raised HbA1c or glucose is enough to diagnose diabetes only when the person has symptoms; without symptoms a second confirmatory test is needed.
thinking: Months of thirst and frequent urination ↓ Obesity and family history are risk factors ↓ Recurrent balanitis reflects glycosuria ↓ Two diagnostic HbA1c results, no ketones ↓ Gradual onset in a middle-aged adult fits type 2 diabetes
exam_trap: B, Type 1 diabetes mellitus — any adult with osmotic symptoms can have it, but the absence of ketones, gradual onset and strong type 2 risk profile make it far less likely.
takeaway: Gradual hyperglycaemic symptoms in an obese middle-aged adult with confirmed raised HbA1c and no ketones indicate type 2 diabetes.

stem:
A 39-year-old teacher has been on three antihypertensive drugs since her twenties without reaching target blood pressure. She now reports cramps in her legs and episodes where her limbs feel heavy and weak. Her potassium is low on repeated samples, although she takes no diuretic and has no diarrhoea or vomiting.

Overproduction of which hormone is most likely?
why_correct: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to retain sodium and excrete potassium, giving hypertension that is hard to control and spontaneous hypokalaemia with cramps and weakness. Early-onset resistant hypertension with low potassium and no diuretic is the classic pattern of primary hyperaldosteronism, the commonest secondary cause of hypertension.
why_wrong: B. Cortisol excess can cause hypertension and low potassium, but would bring Cushingoid features such as striae, central weight gain and bruising. C. Adrenaline excess (phaeochromocytoma) causes paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations rather than persistent hypokalaemia. D. Thyroxine excess raises systolic pressure with weight loss, tremor and tachycardia, not hypokalaemia. E. Growth hormone excess causes acromegalic features, not isolated hypokalaemic hypertension.
pearl: Primary hyperaldosteronism may be due to a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma, which can be cured by adrenalectomy, or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, which is treated medically with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; adrenal vein sampling distinguishes the two before surgery.
thinking: Young woman with resistant hypertension ↓ Cramps and weakness from low potassium ↓ No diuretic or GI loss to explain it ↓ Sodium retention plus potassium wasting ↓ Mineralocorticoid excess: aldosterone
exam_trap: B, Cortisol — it also has mineralocorticoid effects at high levels, but without any Cushingoid features aldosterone is far more likely.
takeaway: Resistant hypertension with unexplained hypokalaemia should prompt thoughts of aldosterone excess.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected: adrenal vein sampling separates unilateral adenoma (surgery) from bilateral hyperplasia (MRA); the old wording linked it illogically to bilateral hyperplasia being commoner.

stem:
A 50-year-old man is reviewed in the hypertension clinic because his blood pressure remains high despite an ACE inhibitor, a calcium-channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic at full doses. His adherence has been confirmed. He was found to have a low potassium before the diuretic was started, and an incidental adrenal nodule was seen on a CT scan last year.

Which blood test should be arranged first to look for the most likely secondary cause?
why_correct: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia that predates diuretic use and an adrenal nodule strongly suggests primary hyperaldosteronism. The first-line screening test is the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which is high because aldosterone is autonomously produced and renin is suppressed. Potassium should be corrected and interfering drugs considered before interpreting it.
why_wrong: A. Plasma metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma, which causes paroxysmal symptoms rather than hypokalaemia. B. The dexamethasone suppression test screens for cortisol excess, and there are no Cushingoid features. C. Renin on its own cannot show autonomous aldosterone production; the ratio is needed. E. Thyroid disease does not explain hypokalaemia with an adrenal nodule.
pearl: A positive aldosterone-to-renin ratio needs confirmatory testing (for example saline suppression) and then subtype localisation, usually with adrenal imaging and adrenal vein sampling, in a specialist centre.
thinking: Resistant hypertension despite three drugs ↓ Hypokalaemia before any diuretic ↓ Adrenal nodule on imaging ↓ Suspect primary hyperaldosteronism ↓ Screen with aldosterone-to-renin ratio
exam_trap: A, Plasma metanephrines — an adrenal nodule with hypertension brings phaeochromocytoma to mind, but the low potassium points to aldosterone excess and he has no paroxysmal symptoms.
takeaway: Screen for primary hyperaldosteronism with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

stem:
At an NHS Health Check, a 45-year-old office worker asks which aspects of his lifestyle and health make diabetes more likely in his case. He walks to work, eats a mostly Mediterranean-style diet, but his waist circumference has increased steadily over the past decade.

Which feature most increases his risk of developing type 2 diabetes?

options.B: Diet high in fruit and vegetables
options.E: A body mass index in the low-normal range

why_correct: Excess body fat, particularly visceral fat around the abdomen, drives insulin resistance and is the most important modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes. A rising waist circumference is a strong marker of this risk even when other habits are healthy.
why_wrong: A. Regular physical activity improves insulin sensitivity and lowers risk. B. A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and fibre is protective. D. High insulin sensitivity is the opposite of the insulin resistance that underlies type 2 diabetes. E. A low-normal BMI is associated with lower, not higher, risk.
pearl: People of South Asian, Chinese, African-Caribbean and Black African origin develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMI thresholds, so NICE uses lower BMI cut-offs to define overweight in these groups.
thinking: Asks about personal diabetes risk ↓ Healthy activity and diet are protective ↓ Waist size rising over years ↓ Visceral fat drives insulin resistance ↓ Central obesity is the key risk factor
exam_trap: D, High insulin sensitivity — the term sounds medical and relevant, but it describes a protective state; insulin resistance is what causes risk.
takeaway: Central obesity is the major modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes.

stem:
A 69-year-old lifelong smoker is admitted from his GP with lethargy and a cough. Blood tests show a low sodium with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine; he is clinically euvolaemic and takes no diuretics. A chest X-ray shows a hilar mass.

How does the lung abnormality most likely relate to his electrolyte disturbance?

options.A: The mass is causing adrenal failure through direct compression
options.B: The lung lesion is producing or provoking inappropriate ADH release
options.C: Lung tumours cause cranial diabetes insipidus by blocking ADH
options.D: Hypoxia stops the kidney from reabsorbing sodium
options.E: The tumour secretes parathyroid hormone-related peptide which lowers sodium

correct_answer: B. The lung lesion is producing or provoking inappropriate ADH release
why_correct: Low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine in a euvolaemic patient is the pattern of SIADH. Lung disease, especially small cell carcinoma (often a central hilar mass in a smoker) but also pneumonia and other chest pathology, can cause ectopic or inappropriate ADH release, leading to water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.
why_wrong: A. A lung mass does not compress the adrenals; adrenal metastases rarely cause insufficiency, and that is not the mechanism here. C. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine and high sodium, the opposite picture. D. Hypoxia does not directly cause renal sodium wasting; the problem is excess water retention. E. PTHrP causes hypercalcaemia (typically from squamous cell carcinoma), not hyponatraemia.
pearl: Small cell lung cancer is the classic malignant cause of SIADH, while squamous cell carcinoma is linked with PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.
thinking: Hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality ↓ Urine inappropriately concentrated ↓ Euvolaemic, no diuretics: SIADH ↓ Hilar mass in a smoker suggests small cell carcinoma ↓ Tumour drives inappropriate ADH release
exam_trap: E, Parathyroid hormone-related peptide — it is the best-known paraneoplastic hormone from lung cancer, but it causes high calcium rather than low sodium.
takeaway: A lung lesion with euvolaemic hyponatraemia suggests SIADH from inappropriate ADH release.

stem:
A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department from a music festival. Friends say he took ecstasy several hours ago and has since drunk bottle after bottle of water. He became confused, vomited, and then had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting two minutes in the ambulance. He is now drowsy but protecting his airway, and his capillary glucose is normal. His laboratory sodium is 118 mmol/L.

How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: Mild hyponatraemia; the seizure is probably due to another cause
options.B: Pseudohyponatraemia until a repeat sample proves otherwise
options.C: Chronic hyponatraemia to be managed with fluid restriction alone
options.D: Severe hyponatraemia with life-threatening neurological symptoms needing emergency treatment
options.E: Moderate hyponatraemia best treated by stopping oral intake

correct_answer: D. Severe hyponatraemia with life-threatening neurological symptoms needing emergency treatment
why_correct: A sodium this low with a seizure, vomiting and reduced consciousness indicates severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema; MDMA promotes ADH release while heavy water intake dilutes the plasma. This is a medical emergency, treated with boluses of hypertonic saline in a monitored setting aiming for a modest early rise, while keeping the overall correction within safe limits to avoid osmotic demyelination.
why_wrong: A. This degree of hyponatraemia is severe, and it readily explains the seizure. B. Pseudohyponatraemia occurs with marked hyperlipidaemia or paraproteinaemia and would not cause seizures; waiting would delay life-saving treatment. C. This has developed over hours, and fluid restriction alone is far too slow when there are severe neurological symptoms. E. Stopping oral intake is not a treatment in itself and the sodium level is in the severe range.
pearl: Even when hyponatraemia is chronic, severe symptoms such as seizures or reduced consciousness need hypertonic saline, but total correction in the first 24 hours must be limited to reduce the risk of osmotic demyelination.
thinking: Ecstasy plus large water intake ↓ Confusion, vomiting and a seizure ↓ Very low sodium on laboratory sample, glucose normal ↓ Neurological symptoms mean cerebral oedema ↓ Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia is an emergency
exam_trap: A, Mild hyponatraemia; the seizure is probably due to another cause — recreational drugs can provoke seizures directly, but a sodium this low with vomiting and confusion fully explains the fit and needs urgent hypertonic saline.
takeaway: Hyponatraemia with seizures or reduced consciousness is a medical emergency.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem re-set (MDMA/water-loading at a festival) because it nearly reproduced live PAQ15474 (elderly woman, seizure, vomiting, Na 116); thinking, exam_trap and why_wrong C/E realigned.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman who has taken levothyroxine for Hashimoto thyroiditis for years tells her GP that she has lost weight, feels light-headed whenever she stands, and that her gums and palm creases have darkened even though she has not been in the sun. Her blood pressure falls on standing.

Which coexisting autoimmune endocrine condition is most likely?
why_correct: Hyperpigmentation of mucosa and palmar creases from raised ACTH, postural hypotension and weight loss are classic features of primary adrenal insufficiency. Autoimmune Addison's disease commonly clusters with autoimmune thyroid disease (autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2), so new symptoms in someone with Hashimoto thyroiditis should prompt this diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease is autoimmune and can cause weight loss, but not pigmentation or postural hypotension, and it is not endocrine. B. Primary hyperparathyroidism is rarely autoimmune and causes hypercalcaemic symptoms. D. Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension, not postural hypotension with pigmentation. E. Type 1 diabetes is associated with thyroid autoimmunity but would cause osmotic symptoms, not pigmentation.
pearl: In a patient on levothyroxine who develops adrenal insufficiency, steroid replacement must be started before or with any thyroxine increase, because raising thyroxine first can precipitate an adrenal crisis.
thinking: Known autoimmune thyroid disease ↓ Weight loss and postural light-headedness ↓ Pigmented gums and palm creases ↓ Points to raised ACTH from adrenal failure ↓ Autoimmune Addison's disease
exam_trap: E, Type 1 diabetes mellitus — it is the most familiar autoimmune endocrine partner of thyroid disease, but it does not explain pigmentation or a postural drop.
takeaway: Pigmentation and postural hypotension in someone with autoimmune thyroid disease suggests Addison's disease.

stem:
During an annual diabetes foot check at his GP practice, a 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for twenty years is found to have a punched-out ulcer over the first metatarsal head that he had not noticed. The surrounding callus is thick, the foot is warm with palpable pulses, and he cannot feel a 10 g monofilament on either sole.

What is the main underlying factor in this ulcer?

options.E: Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy

correct_answer: E. Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
why_correct: A painless ulcer at a pressure point with heavy callus, warm well-perfused foot and absent monofilament sensation is a neuropathic ulcer. Diabetic sensory neuropathy removes protective sensation, so repeated pressure and minor trauma go unnoticed and break down the skin.
why_wrong: A. Ischaemic ulcers are painful, occur at the toes or heel edges, and the foot is cool with weak pulses; his pulses are palpable. B. Charcot foot causes a hot, swollen, deformed foot and may coexist, but the ulcer itself results from sensory loss. C. Gout causes painful inflamed joints or tophi, not painless plantar ulcers. D. Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter area of the lower leg, not on the sole.
pearl: Any diabetic foot ulcer should prompt referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service, and any new ulcer with spreading infection or ischaemia needs same-day assessment.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ Painless ulcer at a pressure point under callus ↓ Warm foot with good pulses ↓ Absent monofilament sensation ↓ Neuropathy, not ischaemia, is the cause
exam_trap: A, Critical limb ischaemia — diabetes is a strong risk factor for arterial disease, but palpable pulses, a warm foot and a painless plantar ulcer point to neuropathy.
takeaway: A painless plantar ulcer in a warm, well-perfused diabetic foot is neuropathic.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has needed prednisolone at moderate to high doses for most of the past year to control polymyalgia rheumatica. At a rheumatology review she has a rounded face, a fat pad between her shoulders, purple abdominal striae and thin skin that bruises easily.

What is the mechanism behind these features?

options.A: Overproduction of ACTH by a pituitary adenoma
options.B: Ectopic ACTH from an occult tumour

correct_answer: E. Prolonged exposure to exogenous glucocorticoid
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroid treatment is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome. The features arise directly from excess glucocorticoid action on fat distribution, protein catabolism and connective tissue, and endogenous ACTH is actually suppressed by the exogenous steroid.
why_wrong: A. Pituitary ACTH is suppressed, not increased, by prolonged prednisolone. B. Ectopic ACTH is a rare cause and is not needed to explain features in someone on high-dose steroids. C. Prednisolone has modest mineralocorticoid activity, but that does not cause striae, bruising or fat redistribution. D. Steroids do not cause hypothyroidism, and hypothyroidism would not produce these features.
pearl: Because ACTH is suppressed, long-term steroids must not be stopped abruptly; people on prolonged courses should carry a steroid emergency card and receive sick day rules.
thinking: Months of high-dose prednisolone ↓ Moon face, buffalo hump, striae, bruising ↓ Classic Cushingoid features ↓ Endogenous ACTH is suppressed by the drug ↓ Cause is exogenous glucocorticoid excess
exam_trap: A, Overproduction of ACTH by a pituitary adenoma — Cushing disease is the classic endogenous cause, but in a patient taking high-dose steroids the drug itself is the explanation and her ACTH will be low.
takeaway: Cushingoid features on long-term steroids reflect exogenous glucocorticoid excess.

stem:
A 37-year-old office manager who does not have diabetes describes episodes of shakiness, clamminess and a racing heart that come on two to four hours after large pasta or bread-heavy lunches. The episodes never occur when fasting overnight and settle within minutes of eating a snack. She has had no gastric surgery.

Which condition best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Adrenergic symptoms occurring a few hours after a carbohydrate-rich meal, relieved by eating and never seen when fasting, suggest reactive (postprandial) hypoglycaemia. An exaggerated or delayed insulin response causes glucose to fall below normal after the initial post-meal rise.
why_wrong: A. Thyrotoxicosis causes persistent rather than meal-linked symptoms, with weight loss and heat intolerance. B. Phaeochromocytoma attacks are not tied to carbohydrate meals and include headache and hypertension. D. Insulinoma typically causes fasting hypoglycaemia, and her episodes never occur overnight. E. Panic disorder would not have such a consistent relation to meals or be relieved by food.
pearl: Postprandial hypoglycaemia is also seen after gastric surgery (late dumping), so ask about previous upper gastrointestinal operations including bariatric procedures.
thinking: No diabetes ↓ Adrenergic symptoms hours after high-carbohydrate meals ↓ Never fasting, relieved by food ↓ No previous gastric surgery ↓ Reactive hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: D, Insulinoma — it is the textbook cause of hypoglycaemia in someone without diabetes, but it characteristically causes fasting rather than post-meal episodes.
takeaway: Hypoglycaemic symptoms that follow carbohydrate meals and not fasting suggest reactive hypoglycaemia.

stem:
A 29-year-old man without diabetes keeps telling his GP that he has spells of sweating and feeling muddled which he believes are 'low sugar attacks' because a chocolate bar helps. Before arranging specialist tests, the GP wants to know what would confirm that genuine hypoglycaemia is occurring.

Which combination of findings is required?

options.A: Symptoms that improve after eating, with no glucose measured
options.B: Hypoglycaemic symptoms, a documented low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is raised
options.C: A low glucose on one routine fasting sample without symptoms
options.D: Palpitations, headache and hypertension during attacks
options.E: Weight loss, thirst and polyuria over several weeks

correct_answer: B. Hypoglycaemic symptoms, a documented low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is raised
why_correct: Whipple's triad confirms clinically significant hypoglycaemia: symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia, a low plasma glucose measured during those symptoms, and resolution of symptoms once glucose is raised. All three elements are needed before investigating causes such as insulinoma.
why_wrong: A. Feeling better after food is non-specific and does not prove a low glucose. C. An isolated low reading without symptoms may be artefactual or of no clinical significance. D. Headache, palpitations and hypertension suggest phaeochromocytoma. E. Weight loss, thirst and polyuria indicate hyperglycaemia rather than hypoglycaemia.
pearl: In suspected spontaneous hypoglycaemia, the definitive test is a supervised prolonged fast, measuring glucose, insulin, C-peptide and a sulfonylurea screen during a documented low.
thinking: Episodic symptoms attributed to low sugar ↓ Needs proof before investigation ↓ Symptoms must coincide with low glucose ↓ And resolve when glucose is corrected ↓ Whipple's triad
exam_trap: A, Symptoms that improve after eating — this is what the patient reports, but without a measured low glucose it cannot confirm hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: Genuine hypoglycaemia is confirmed by Whipple's triad: symptoms, low measured glucose, and relief with glucose.

presentation: Hypoglycaemia in a person with diabetes
stem:
Mid-afternoon at a building site, a 61-year-old bricklayer who takes gliclazide and metformin for type 2 diabetes becomes pale, sweaty and shaky, and says his heart is pounding. He skipped lunch because he was busy. A colleague calls NHS 111 for advice.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Sweating, tremor, pallor and palpitations are adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia. Gliclazide, a sulfonylurea, stimulates insulin release regardless of glucose level, so missing a meal while still working physically makes a low glucose very likely. He should take fast-acting glucose and have his capillary glucose checked.
why_wrong: A. Acute coronary syndrome can cause sweating, but chest pain would be expected and the missed meal with a sulfonylurea points elsewhere. B. DKA develops over hours to days with thirst, vomiting and ketotic breathing, and is uncommon in type 2 diabetes on these drugs. C. Heat exhaustion causes weakness and sweating but not this sudden adrenergic picture after a missed meal. E. HHS evolves over days with dehydration and confusion, not acute shakiness.
pearl: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia can be prolonged or recur after initial treatment, especially in older people or those with reduced renal function, so observation may be needed.
